newsitem.title: USA: Sun-Diamond goes on trial in Espy probe.
newsitem.headline: Sun-Diamond goes on trial in Espy probe.

text.p: Sun-Diamond Growers of California went to court on Monday in the first trial resulting from the government's investigation of former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy as a related probe of giant chicken processor Tyson Foods neared completion.

The action against two major agribusiness firms marks a new phase of the two-year investigation that legal sources have said is pointing to a criminal indictment of Espy, former cabinet member and associate of President Bill Clinton's.
Espy resigned as head of the huge agriculture agency in 1994 after being accused of illegally accepting gifts and favors from companies and concerns his agency regulated.
The special investigation of Espy, led by Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz, has resulted in four sets of indictments and charges against a dozen individuals and concerns.
Sun-Diamond is charged with trying to gain influence with Espy by plying him and his girlfriend with expensive gifts and favors, and through illegal campaign contributions to Espy's brother Henry.

The trial in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia is expected to last two to three weeks and Monday's opening day was taken up with interviews of 70 prospective jurists. Opening statements could be made Tuesday.

Tyson Foods -- the giant Arkansas-based poultry processor that has enjoyed close ties with Clinton since he was Arkansas governor -- was singled out early on in the controversy for giving gifts to Espy in the form of sports tickets, transportation and other entertainment.
It is also said to have awarded Espy's girlfriend a Tyson Foundation scholarship and provided her with transportation to events with Espy.

The Agriculture Department was considering tightening regulations on the poultry industry at the time, and allegations were that Tyson Foods was trying to use its clout with the White House and Espy to soften the plans.
No indictments have been filed against Tyson Foods, but Smaltz and his team have been conducting an aggressive investigation into the company and its dealings with Espy.

Sources familiar with the investigation said that Jack Williams, Washington lobbyist for Tyson, is a key focus in the investigation, and legal experts speculated that it could only be a matter of time before Williams is indicted.
Williams was not available for comment, but his attorney Hank Schuelke said that given Smaltz's track record, he would not be surprised if an indictment were returned soon.
Tyson officials have denied any wrongdoing, and have said they will fight any indictments to the "bitter end".

Legal experts said a weekend ruling by Sun-Diamond presiding judge Ricardo Urbina against the company's motion to dismiss the trial was significant for the California concern, and may have ramifications for Tyson Foods.
Urbina dismissed Sun-Diamond's stance that a gratuity has to be given to get a specific action. He said if the gratuity is given solely due to the official's position, it is illegal.
He also ruled that gifts to Espy's girlfriend are suspect because they provided companionship, a "thing of value".
